paras: The Henderson whitecapping shooting took place late on the night of October 6, 1903, at Henderson, Texas, when Bob Willis, a Black man, fired on a party of young white men who had come to his home to flog him, killing one and wounding another. The dead man was Charles Brown, and the sheriff took Willis into custody. The story ran nationally, and the Salt Lake Herald and the Black weeklies Richmond Planet and Cleveland Gazette praised Willis for defending himself.

Henderson was the county seat of Rusk County, Texas. The dispatches gave no reason for the attempted flogging beyond "some alleged offense, not clearly stated"; a Dallas report said the offense was "not yet learned here."

In the same weeks Rusk County was the scene of a campaign of whippings of Black residents. Webster Flanagan, the federal revenue collector at Austin, reported on October 14 that white men had whipped two Black men with a nail-studded strap, one fatally, and that all Black people had been ordered to leave the county; he did not mention Willis. R. T. Milner of the Henderson Times wrote that the trouble had begun "several weeks ago" in the town with the whipping of Black residents warned "that they must go to work."

According to the Associated Press dispatch from Henderson, the party of young white men reached Willis's home late on Tuesday night, October 6. Willis warned them not to approach, and when they kept advancing he fired. The shots killed Charles Brown, "a young man recently from Georgia," and wounded a young man whose name the papers printed as Gossett, Gorsett, Garsett, Gersett and Garrett.
A separate Dallas report placed the attack at Willis's cabin, said the second man was "badly" wounded, and added that the mob fled and the sheriff took Willis in charge before it could regroup.

Willis remained in the sheriff's hands, and the Dallas report said the sheriff "has since protected him" and that there seemed to be "no disposition to lynch him." The version printed in southern papers and later in the Black weeklies added that the sheriff "will probably spirit him away" that night. No report of an inquest into Brown's death, a grand jury inquiry, a trial or Willis's later fate appears in the coverage. The Salt Lake Herald predicted that even if freed Willis would have to leave, since "some friend of the outlaw who was killed will kill Willis."

The Associated Press story ran on October 8 and 9 in papers from Georgia, Alabama and Virginia to Indiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, Montana and Utah. Southern headlines put the dead white man first: the Birmingham Age-Herald ran "Negro Shoots White Man," and the Savannah Morning News added a subhead noting that Brown was a "Native of Georgia." The Montgomery Advertiser and the Daily Ardmoreite, by contrast, named the attackers as whitecappers, with "Negro Fires on Whitescappers" and "Fatal Whitecapping." Several northern and western papers cast Willis as the defender: "Negro Defends Self," "Negro Protected Himself."

On October 9 the Salt Lake Herald devoted an editorial, "The Case of Willis," to the shooting, calling the mob "a gang of lawless desperadoes" and saying it was "at a loss to understand" why Willis had been arrested.

The Black press took the southern wire text, with its spelling "Bob Williams," and added open approval. On October 10 the Richmond Planet printed the dispatch and declared that Willis "was strictly within the letter of the law, and he knew how to shoot." Under the heading "Knew When to Shoot," it advised "respectable, law-abiding" Black southerners to keep "a good shot-gun or a repeating rifle." The Cleveland Gazette ran the story on October 24 under the headline "Shot and Killed by a Mobocrat, Good!", rewriting the floggers as "young white brutes" and Willis as "an Afro-American." The Sedalia Weekly Conservator later reprinted Milner's denunciation of the Rusk County whippings, without reference to Willis.

Most copies of the dispatch and the Dallas report called the man "Bob Willis," while the Savannah Morning News, the Richmond Planet and the Cleveland Gazette called him "Bob Williams." The wounded man appears as Gossett, Gorsett, Garsett, Gersett and Garrett, with no first name.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Henderson
accounts.gist: Young white men went at night to flog Willis for an unstated offense; he warned them, fired as they advanced, killing Brown and wounding a second man, and was in the sheriff's hands; the southern version added that the sheriff would probably spirit him away.

accounts.label: Dallas dispatch
accounts.gist: A 'fatal whitecapping affair': the mob came to Willis's cabin, he killed Brown and badly wounded Garrett, the mob fled, and the sheriff took and protected him, with 'no disposition to lynch him'.

accounts.label: Black weekly rewrite
accounts.gist: The Cleveland Gazette retold the wire calling the party 'young white brutes' and Willis 'an Afro-American', under a headline cheering the shooting.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP text verbatim; southern headlines stressed the dead white man ('Negro Shoots White Man'; Savannah's subhead 'Charles Brown, Who Was Killed, Native of Georgia').
Several northern and western headlines cast Willis as defending himself: 'Negro Defends Self', 'Negro Protected Himself', 'Man Who Would Flog Negro Is Now Dead'.
The Salt Lake Herald editorial called the mob 'a gang of lawless desperadoes' and said Willis should be freed at once.
The Richmond Planet praised Willis as 'strictly within the letter of the law' and urged armed self-defense against the 'white hoodlum element'.
The Cleveland Gazette headed its item 'Shot and Killed by a Mobocrat, Good!' and called the floggers 'young white brutes'.

conflicts.note: The 'Williams' form appears in the southern AP version (Savannah, Montgomery, Richmond, Birmingham) and the two Black weeklies that reprinted it; the separate Dallas dispatch and most other AP copies have 'Willis'.
Variant spellings of one wounded man; no paper gives a first name.

versions.value: has since protected him; no disposition to lynch

conflicts.note: Not contradictory: one reports protection in place, the other an expected removal; no later report says where Willis was taken.

record_check.record: Bob Willis, Charles Brown, Garrett, Gersett
record_check.dossier: Bob Willis is the only target of the attack; Charles Brown was a member of the flogging party who was killed, and Garrett and Gersett are spellings of one wounded member of the party.
Attempted flogging (no whipping took place); Willis shot two of the party, killing one.
A party of young white men; Charles Brown and Gossett/Garrett are named.
Willis was not in custody when attacked, but was taken into the sheriff's custody afterward.
Rusk, supported only by later reports calling Henderson the county seat of Rusk County.
Richmond Planet (one editorial spread over two items) and Cleveland Gazette a22; Cleveland Gazette a21 and the St. Paul Appeal item are not about this episode.

info: Late on the night of Tuesday, October 6, 1903 ('late last night' in October 7 dispatches; 'the 6th' in the Cleveland Gazette)
Willis's home, called a cabin in the Dallas report, at Henderson, Texas
Bob Willis (printed 'Bob Williams' in several papers), 'a negro', the target of the attempted flogging; he was not reported hurt
'some alleged offense, not clearly stated'; the Dallas report said the offense was 'not yet learned here'
A party of young white men, unnamed except Charles Brown, who was killed, and the wounded man (Gossett/Gorsett/Garsett/Gersett/Garrett)
No report of an inquest, grand jury action, trial or Willis's later fate was found
